newsitem.title: USA: Mass. legislators okay new funding for Big Dig.
newsitem.headline: Mass. legislators okay new funding for Big Dig.

text.p: Landmark legislation heads to Gov. William Weld's desk after Massachusetts lawmakers approved a bill that organizes a highway network around Boston to help pay for the Third Harbor Tunnel/Central Artery Project with toll revenues.

Massachusetts is struggling to find a financing mechanism to fund its share of the $10.7 billion project which is known locally as the Big Dig. Originally, Beacon Hill had to find 15 percent of the funding, but under various Federal Highway System proposals being debated in Congress, the state's share could climb to as much as 25 percent.

The measure, which was passed after much debate in the House, 121-28 on Thursday, puts the Massachusetts Turnpike Authority of the new highway system. The law allows the Turnpike Authority to raise tolls as necessary to back bonds to finance the state's share of the Big Dig debt.
"The state is going to raise $25 million to $50 million in tolls and use that to fund its $450 million obligation," said Rep. John Slattery, D-Essex, who spoke out against the measure.
Another lawmaker who expressed concern about the toll hikes, Rep. Robert DeLeo, D-Suffolk said, "The reality is we are looking at possible increase of 200 percent."

On the Senate side, there was also vigorous opposition from legislators representing the areas north and west of Boston, who argued that the measure unfairly places the sole burden of paying for the Big Dig on their constituents.
"Why should one group of people that travel along the highway be asked time and time again to underwrite other highways?" argued Sen. Warren Tolman, D-Watertown.

In the end the measure passed both houses. It allows toll revenues from the Sumner and Ted Williams tunnels, the Tobin Bridge and the eastern section of the Turnpike all to be used to fund the state's share of the Big Dig. It places responsibility for the project under the Turnpike Authority.

Written by Gov. Weld and Transporation Secretary James Kerasiotes, the measure allows Massachusetts to pay 25 percent of the remaining $5.5 billion to be spent on the project. Federal transportation officials, who will contribute the rest of the financing, have required the state to submit a comprehensive financing plan by April 1.
